title: implement intersect_ray_1d

atoms.evidence: markdown sets R(u)=O+uD vs O(v)=L_1+v(L_2-L_1); learner must internalize the form to derive the 2x2 system
the whole exercise derives uD - v(L1-L2) = L1-O and solves the 2x2 system; this atom IS the exercise
mat = t.stack([D, L_1 - L_2], dim=-1); dedicated 'Aside - difference between stack and concatenate' dropdown teaches the distinction
O, D = ray and L_1, L_2 = segment — first-axis Python unpacking after slicing to 2D
sol = t.linalg.solve(mat, vec) — unbatched scalar instance, but the API is the same; this exercise introduces the function
try: sol = t.linalg.solve(...); except RuntimeError: return False — exercise dropdown 'Failing Solve' explicitly directs the learner to catch the exception
ray = ray[:, :2] and segment = segment[:, :2] discard the z dim via basic indexing — view, no mutation, so this is the slice-as-view side of the atom

notes: Introduces three load-bearing atoms (segment-line-intersect-2d, linalg-solve-batched, try-except-solve) in one exercise. The try-except path is the explicit lesson — it's the manual scalar fallback that 0_1_2 replaces with singular-matrix-mask-trick. Confirms stack-vs-cat: the exercise teaches it via dedicated aside, which is unusual.
